headline: New Hampshire Democrats draft cannabis legalization bill after wins
dek: Rep. Jared Sullivan is drafting an adult-use cannabis bill after Democrats won both chambers, but re-elected Gov. Kelly Ayotte still opposes legalization.
key_points: Democrats are projected to hold 292 of 400 House seats and 15 of 24 Senate seats in New Hampshire after the 3 November election.
Rep. Jared Sullivan, who sponsored the House-passed HB 186 this year, is drafting a new legalization bill and says he is open to negotiating with Republicans.

Republican Gov. Kelly Ayotte won re-election and still opposes legalization; overriding a veto needs two-thirds of each chamber, which in the Senate means at least one Republican vote if all 24 members vote.
New Hampshire is the only New England state without legal adult-use cannabis.
body: New Hampshire's long-running cannabis stalemate has a new set of players. After Democrats won control of both legislative chambers on 3 November, state Rep. Jared Sullivan said he is drafting a fresh bill to legalize and regulate adult-use cannabis, The Marijuana Herald reported, citing an interview with WMUR.

The obstacle that remains is the governor. Republican Kelly Ayotte won re-election and continues to oppose recreational legalization. That turns the coming session into a test of whether Democrats can either win her over with a narrower design or assemble the two-thirds majorities needed to override a veto.
Democrats are projected to hold 292 of the 400 seats in the House and 15 of the 24 seats in the Senate, according to the Herald. That is a decisive House majority and a narrower Senate one.

Overriding a veto requires two-thirds of those voting in each chamber. In a full 24-member Senate that means 16 votes, so even if every Democrat backs a bill, at least one Republican senator would have to join them. The House majority is large enough that an override there is plausible on paper; it is the Senate that would decide the question.

There is a recent precedent for that kind of coalition. In August, lawmakers overrode Ayotte's veto of SB 468, a narrower bill letting medical cannabis producers grow in greenhouses. The Senate vote was 16 to 8, with eight Democrats and eight Republicans in favour, and the House vote was 257 to 44, according to the Marijuana Policy Project.
> In New Hampshire the House has never been the problem. The question is whether one Republican senator, or the governor, will move.

The House has passed legalization bills repeatedly in recent years, only for the Senate to stop them. This year's attempt, HB 186, would have legalized possession and sales for adults 21 and over and created a regulated market. The House approved it in January; in March the then Republican-controlled Senate voted 15 to 9 to table it. A House-passed bill met the same fate in 2025, when the Senate tabled it 12 to 10, according to our New Hampshire legal hub.

Sullivan sponsored HB 186. Speaking to WMUR, he signalled flexibility, saying there is room for negotiation if it makes a bill bipartisan. Some Democrats want to work directly with Ayotte rather than plan around an override.

New Hampshire already decriminalized small amounts: since 2017, possessing three-quarters of an ounce or less has been a civil violation punishable by a fine rather than a crime. Its medical programme, created in 2013, lets certified patients buy from nonprofit Alternative Treatment Centers, which operate seven dispensary locations. Since October 2024, providers can certify adults for any debilitating or terminal condition in their judgment. Home growing is not allowed, even for patients.

That leaves the state as the only one in New England without legal adult-use sales. Every neighbouring state, Maine, Massachusetts and Vermont, has licensed stores, and Massachusetts voters on 3 November rejected an attempt to end adult-use sales there by roughly three to one. For legalization supporters in Concord, that makes New Hampshire an island in a region that has settled the question.

The Marijuana Herald lists New Hampshire among the states most likely to legalize adult-use cannabis in 2027, alongside Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. In both of those states, as we reported on 6 November, Democrats also gained legislative ground in the election. New Hampshire differs because of its governor: in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin the obstacles have been legislative, while in Concord the main barrier now sits in the corner office.

The shape of the bill will matter as much as the votes. Sullivan's openness to negotiation suggests the draft could move away from HB 186's regulated-market design to win Republican support. How far it moves, and whether that is enough for Ayotte or a single Republican senator, is the detail operators and advocates should read first.

First, the text of Sullivan's draft when it is filed for the 2027 session, and in particular how it structures licensing and taxes compared with HB 186. Second, any statement from Ayotte that softens or hardens her position. Third, how the Senate's nine Republicans respond: one vote is the difference between a bill that can survive a veto and one that cannot. Until then, the legal status in New Hampshire is unchanged, and our state hub will track the bill as it moves.
